newsitem.title: TURKEY: Beleaguered Erbakan hosts Moslem nations' summit.
newsitem.headline: Beleaguered Erbakan hosts Moslem nations' summit.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, beset by a range of domestic woes, on Saturday opened a ministerial meeting of eight Moslem countries in Istanbul in preparation for a summit which he has masterminded.

The meeting is set to launch the Developing-Eight (D-8) economic cooperation group, bringing together Bangladesh, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Turkey to develop trade, industry and financial projects.
"The D-8 will take on an important role in solving the problems of humanity in our globalising world," Erbakan told a meeting of foreign ministers from the eight countries in an opening address.
But doubts about Erbakan's hold on power and foreign criticism of Turkey's military incursion into northern Iraq have overshadowed hopes of economic gains among member countries.

On Saturday a glum Erbakan, struggling to save his crumbling coalition, sat alone at the head of the conference table for half an hour waiting for the arrival of ministers, including his deputy and foreign minister, Tansu Ciller.
Ciller held a news conference at the summit in the afternoon where she made no refernce to the D-8, but repeated calls for elections to resolve the political crisis.

She is hoping to take over the prime minister's post by the end of the month to solve a crisis over Islamist activism which has distracted domestic attention away from Erbakan's brainchild, the D-8 Group.
"Even Erbakan has forgotten it," said a headline in Radikal newspaper. "Turkey has shown no interest in the founding summit of the D-8, which it initiated itself," Deniz Zeyrek said in the article.

Erbakan has described D-8 as "a turning point in human history", but others are less enthusiastic about his promise to create an Islamic "Common Market" and turn the Turkish republic away from its traditional Western vocation.
"D-8 is an organisation of the new world. God willing, this group will play a big role in bringing peace and security," he said ahead of talks with Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif.
Heads of state or government are scheduled to meet on Sunday for the final summit day, but not all countries have sent their leaders. Nigeria's delegation was to be headed by its industry minister.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak was staying away following a row between Cairo and Ankara over Turkey's Iraq operation and growing Turkish-Israeli military cooperation. Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri and Foreign Minister Amr Moussa are representing Egypt.
Thousands of Turkish troops poured into northern Iraq on May 14 in an anti-guerrilla operation condemned by the Arab League and some of Turkey's neighbours, including Iran.
Outgoing Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani was due to attend the summit despite fresh tension with Turkey over Iran's alleged support for the rebel Kurdistan Workers Party.

Erbakan visited all D-8 countries except Bangladesh soon after coming to power last June. He fostered economic links with projects such as a $23 billion gas deal with Iran, drawing strong criticism from NATO-member Turkey's Western allies.

Political analysts say the D-8 group, devised as a potential developing world partner to the G-7 group of rich countries, has been ill-thought-out in Erbakan's haste to strengthen Turkey's links with the Islamic world.

Domestically, Erbakan's vision of Moslem Brotherhood has been reduced to tatters by fierce opposition from the secularist establishment which has brought his 11-month-old coalition to breaking point and prompted him to seek early elections.
Erbakan, facing the possibility of losing power, continued to talk enthusiastically this week about major D-8 projects to build passenger aircraft, helicopters, cars and computers.

Among planned areas of cooperation, Egypt will oversee trade, Turkey will coordinate industry proposals, Pakistan will be responsible for agriculture, Nigeria will oversee energy plans and Indonesia will be responsible for human resources.
Iran will oversee telecommunication projects, Bangladesh will deal with rural development and Malaysia will focus on privatisation, banking and Islamic insurance, or 'takaful'.
